items.title: Book Review: Aziz Abu Sarah and Maoz Inon – The Future is Peace
items.body:
This review was published at The Englewood Review of Books at https://englewoodreview.org/aziz-abu-sarah-and-maoz-inon-the-future-is-peace-feature-review/

A Powerful Witness Through Unlikely Friendship

A Feature Review of

The Future is Peace: A Shared Journey Across the Holy Land
By Aziz Abu Sarah and Maoz Inon

Hardcover: Crown, 2026

Reviewed by John W. Morehead

There are few places in the world where hope seems more fragile than the Holy Land. The attacks of October 7, 2023, the ensuing war in Gaza, the deepening mistrust between Israelis and Palestinians, and the competing narratives surrounding justice and security have convinced many that reconciliation is no longer realistic. Against this backdrop, The Future Is Peace offers a remarkably hopeful counterpoint—not because its authors deny the depth of the conflict, but because they have experienced its tragedies firsthand.

Aziz Abu Sarah, a Palestinian peacebuilder whose brother was killed during the First Intifada, and Maoz Inon, an Israeli entrepreneur whose parents were murdered in the Hamas attacks of October 7, are unlikely companions. They first met nearly a decade ago over tea in Jerusalem through their mutual work in travel and tourism, believing that travel could become a bridge across social divides. Their professional acquaintance deepened after October 7, when Aziz reached out to Maoz with a simple message of condolence. That gesture of compassion led to a three-day meeting in Geneva where the two men shared their grief, wrestled honestly with their pain, and consciously chose reconciliation over revenge. This book is the story of that friendship and an invitation for readers to imagine a different future.

Travel functions as both the literal and the literary framework of the book. The authors journey together through Tel Aviv-Jaffa, Jerusalem, the West Bank, Nazareth, and Galilee, weaving together the histories, memories, and competing narratives that make each place simultaneously beautiful and contested. Yet the geographical journey mirrors a deeper pilgrimage. As they describe it, this is a story of “mutual loss and pain, along with the shared vision of peace” (2). Their travels embody a conviction that “nothing is more powerful or transformative than the experience of stepping out of one’s comfort zone to meet the ‘other’ and truly listening to their story” (3). This commitment to what they call a “dual-narrative approach” becomes the organizing principle of the book.

The authors never underestimate the forces working against such encounters. They write that “we are divided by fear and anger, by extremism and tribalism” (2), realities that have been reinforced across generations. They observe that peace becomes elusive “when each side believes that the other is a threat to its existence” (2). These are not merely political disagreements but existential fears. Throughout the book they return repeatedly to the corrosive effects of mistrust and to the conviction that genuine peace begins with recovering the capacity to encounter one another as human beings rather than enemies.

Readers familiar with the work of the Foundation for Religious Diplomacy (FRD) will recognize significant points of convergence. For more than two decades FRD has argued that lasting peace does not require the elimination of deep differences but the cultivation of trust amid them. Likewise, Aziz and Maoz do not imagine a future without disagreement. Instead, they envision relationships capable of bearing disagreement without collapsing into violence. Their perspective is captured well through their quotation of Pope Francis: “What would a society, a family, or a group of friends be like without tension or conflict? Do you know what it would be? It would be a cemetery: Because only in dead things are there no tensions and no conflicts. When there is life, there is tension, and there is conflict.” It is a striking reminder that peace should not be confused with the absence of tension. Rather, the challenge is learning to inhabit tension without allowing it to become destructive.

The authors are equally honest about the social costs of pursuing this path. Peacebuilders often become objects of suspicion within their own communities, viewed as naïve at best and traitorous at worst. They describe how those who seek reconciliation are frequently accused of undermining their own people or legitimizing the enemy (77). Their concept of “co-resistance,” another element that overlaps with FRD’s approach, captures this delicate balancing act: resisting injustice together without abandoning one’s own community or convictions. This is one of the book’s strongest contributions. Rather than advocating a shallow neutrality, Aziz and Maoz demonstrate that authentic peacemaking often demands greater courage than continued hostility.

What makes the book compelling is precisely what it does not attempt to be. It is not a history of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, nor a policy proposal for resolving it. Aziz and Maoz are not writing as historians, political scientists, military strategists, or scholars of religion. They write as two people whose lives have been shattered by violence and who have become convinced that cycles of revenge cannot secure a future for either of their peoples. Their emphasis therefore falls on grief, trauma, humanization, forgiveness, grassroots initiatives, and the transformative potential of relationships. Their argument is, in essence, that ordinary people must begin creating the relationships that politics has repeatedly failed to produce.

Yet this admirable focus also points toward the book’s principal limitation. One can hardly ask how Israelis and Palestinians might become trustworthy neighbors without eventually confronting a more difficult question: what competing visions of political, religious, and moral order are shaping this conflict? The Future Is Peace clearly acknowledges the brutality of Hamas and the personal devastation its violence has inflicted, particularly through Maoz’s own story. It also offers some critique of broader political leadership on both sides. But it devotes comparatively little sustained attention to Hamas as a theopolitical movement or other challenges such as Israeli Zionist movements, Palestinian Islamist currents beyond Hamas, secular nationalist traditions, and Christian theological interpretations that shape attitudes toward the conflict.

This observation is not a criticism of what the authors set out to accomplish. Their project is intentionally moral and relational rather than ideological. They are addressing a missing dimension of peacebuilding by insisting that relationships matter as much as political agreements. They would likely argue, with considerable justification, that governments, military strategies, and ideological debates have dominated the conversation for decades while relationships have continued to deteriorate. Their response is to begin where trust has collapsed most profoundly: between ordinary people.

Even so, the reverse observation also deserves consideration. Durable peace requires more than transformed relationships. It also requires sustained engagement with the rival theological, political, and historical visions that shape those relationships. Hamas represents more than a terrorist organization; it embodies a comprehensive vision of political and religious legitimacy that cannot simply be dissolved through empathy or friendship. Likewise, elements within Israeli Zionism, Palestinian nationalism, secular political ideologies, and even Christian theological interpretations of the land deserve careful examination as competing visions of justice, sovereignty, and the common good. If these deeper commitments remain unaddressed, peace risks becoming primarily psychological rather than also ideological.

This challenge extends well beyond Israel and Palestine. Many contemporary reconciliation efforts understandably prioritize relationship-building while avoiding deep theological or philosophical contestation for fear that it will fracture fragile trust. Yet in conflicts rooted in ultimate commitments—about God, nation, land, identity, and justice—those commitments cannot remain permanently bracketed. The task is not simply learning to understand one another but learning how to contest profoundly incompatible convictions without resorting to domination or violence.

In this respect, The Future Is Peace raises an important question that it does not fully answer, though perhaps no single book could. How do societies sustain trust when the differences at stake cannot be reconciled? Aziz and Maoz convincingly show that friendship across enemy lines is possible and that reconciliation begins with courageous acts of compassion. They demonstrate that fear and dehumanization need not determine the future. But lasting peace will require not only transformed relationships but also trustworthy ways of engaging rival visions of justice, security, sovereignty, and sacred obligation.

That observation should not diminish the achievement of this remarkable book. Rather, it highlights its greatest contribution. Aziz and Maoz remind readers that no political settlement can endure without people willing to risk trust across deep divides. At a time when public discourse increasingly assumes that those on the other side are existential threats, their friendship offers a powerful witness that another way is possible. If The Future Is Peace leaves readers asking how such trust might also be sustained amid irreconcilable differences, then perhaps it has accomplished something even more valuable: it has moved the conversation from whether peace is possible to what kind of peace will ultimately endure.

items.title: Announcing a New Collaboration with Brigham Young University to Advance Trust Amid Deep Differences
items.body:
We’re pleased to announce that the Foundation for Religious Diplomacy has begun a new collaboration with Brigham Young University’s Social Science and AI Lab (SAIL) to develop the Rivaltrust Builder—an AI-guided formation experience designed to prepare people for meaningful engagement across deep and enduring disagreements.

At a time when many people experience others with different convictions as threatening, FRD is focused on a different question:

Can people build enough trust to sustain cooperation even when they continue to disagree about what matters most?

The Rivaltrust Builder is designed to help individuals:

  • Reflect on the experiences that shaped their convictions

  • Engage differing perspectives with honesty and courage

  • Prepare for real-world conversations marked by tension, not avoidance

This work builds on FRD’s long-standing practice of Heart & Mind Conversations, now translated into a scalable, research-backed digital format.

Development is underway, and we will soon begin inviting participants into early pilot experiences.

If you are interested in participating in future cohorts or learning more, we invite you to stay connected.

items.title: Leonard Swidler has passed
items.body:
Leonard Swidler passed away on March 23. He was was Professor of Catholic Thought and Interreligious Dialogue at Temple University, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where he taught from 1966 to 2022. He was the co-founder (in 1964, with Arlene Swidler) and editor of the Journal of Ecumenical Studies. His work was an important influence on the Foundation for Religious Diplomacy. Swidler was best known for his “Dialogue Decalogue: Ground Rules for Interreligious, Interideological Dialogue.” They are reproduced below. You can download the entire article and discussion of these principles here:

FIRST PRINCIPLE

The essential purpose of dialogue is to learn, which entails change. At the very least, to learn that one’s dialogue partner views the world differently is to effect a change in oneself. Reciprocally, change happens for one’s partner as they learn about themself.

SECOND PRINCIPLE

Dialogue must be a two-sided project: both between religious/ideological groups, and within religious/ideological groups (inter- and intra-). Intra-religious/ideological dialogue is vital for moving one’s community toward an increasingly perceptive insight into reality. 

THIRD PRINCIPLE

It is imperative that each participant comes to the dialogue with complete honesty and sincerity. This means not only describing the major and minor thrusts, as well as potential future shifts of one’s tradition, but also possible difficulties that they have with it. 

FOURTH PRINCIPLE

One must compare only their ideals with their partner’s ideals and their practice with the partner’s practice, not one's ideals with one's partner’s practice.

FIFTH PRINCIPLE

Each participant needs to describe themself. For example, only a Muslim can describe what it really means to be an authentic member of the Muslim community. At the same time, when one’s partner in dialogue attempts to describe back to them what they have understood of their partner’s self-description, then such a description must be recognizable to the described party.

SIXTH PRINCIPLE

Participants must not come to the dialogue with any preconceptions as to where the points of disagreement lie. A process of agreeing with one's partner as much as possible, without violating the integrity of one's own tradition, will reveal where the real boundaries between the traditions lie: the point where they cannot agree without going against the principles of one's own tradition.

SEVENTH PRINCIPLE

Dialogue can take place only between equals, which means that partners learn from each other—par cum pari according to the Second Vatican Council—and do not merely seek to teach one another.

EIGHTH PRINCIPLE

Dialogue can only take place on the basis of mutual trust. Because it is persons, and not entire communities, that enter into dialogue, it is essential for personal trust to be established. To encourage this it is important that less controversial matters are discussed before dealing with more controversial ones.

NINTH PRINCIPLE

Participants in dialogue should have a healthy level of criticism toward their own traditions. A lack of such criticism implies that one’s tradition has all the answers, thus making dialogue not only unnecessary but unfeasible. The primary purpose of dialogue is to learn, which is impossible if one’s tradition is seen as having all the answers.  

TENTH PRINCIPLE

To understand another religion or ideology one must try to experience it from within, which requires a “passing over,” even if only momentarily, into another’s religious or ideological experience.

items.title: When Proclamation is Really Identity Reinforcement
items.body:
A couple of religion in the news items were of special interest to me over the last week or so. Both came to my attention through Pagan social media groups that I’m a part of. (I’ve had a special interest in the study of Paganism and dialogue with Pagans.) And both items were reported in The Wild Hunt website. These incidents, and a similar one from a different religious tradition, provide insights into the need for critical self-reflection in that what we think we are doing in relation to others is actually perceive as something quite different by others.

On February 25The Wild Hunt reported on a clash between would-be Christian evangelists and Pagans at a public venue called The Market in Pickens, South Carolina. A small number of different Christian ministries were involved, and in the process of trying to “proclaim” the gospel as they saw it, they also used the Bible verse Exodus 22:18: “Thou shalt not suffer a witch to live.” The Pagans felt that this was an attack, possibly one that might involve violence, given the particular Bible verse that was used. By contrast, the Christians saw themselves as merely proclaiming their message, and doing so in peaceful fashion. I confirmed this in a series of text message exchanges with one of the leaders of the Christian groups. (Long story short: my attempts at a theological exchange that tried to provide an alternative perspective and approach fell on deaf ears.)

But this wasn’t the only such clash between Christians and Pagans recently. Just today The Wild Hunt reported on evangelical Christian groups targeting two metaphysical shops in Orlando, Florida. Again, an aggressive and confrontational approach was used, with the Christians seeing themselves as faithful messengers opposing evil, and the Pagans feeling like this was an escalation of attacks. (For Pagan perspectives on such encounters see my conversation with Heron Michelle, and Heather Greene.)

This happens repeatedly. In 2021, Heron Michelle’s metaphysical bookstore in Greenville, North Carolina was “evangelized” in aggressive ways similar to the stories above. And it happens with other religious communities as well. Shortly after I first moved to Utah a friend involved in ministry among Latter-day Saints invited me to the Mormon Miracle Pageant in Manti. The LDS Church used to put on outdoor pageants that involved dramatic reenactments of stories in the Book of Mormon and their church’s history. But I wasn’t able to take in much of the pageant as I was distracted by evangelical preachers who cam and stood just outside church property in a public area and held up signs and shouted “sermons”, many times including elements that would be considered derogatory in their criticism of the LDS Church, its founder, and teachings. At one point a young Latter-day Saint got so upset at the preachers that police along the perimeter had to step in.

I’ve done a lot of reflecting on how Christians interact with those in other religions when its done on the sacred turf of others. I’ve written on it quite a bit, particularly on the Moreheads Musings blog I started when I was in seminary. But for the purposes of this post I’ll summarize three points that I hope my fellow evangelicals will consider.

  1. It’s really identity reinforcement, not proclamation. Despite how my fellow evangelicals characterize their efforts as evangelism, it’s really a way of reinforcing their own sense of identity against what they see as an evil spiritual other. When Christians go to the sacred space of others and engage in this kind of aggressive encounter, it’s not so much an attempt at persuasion as it is a way of solidifying one’s own religious convictions by using the other as a foil. Pagans, Latter-day Saints and others don’t see this as bridge building. It’s fence or wall building that reinforces the religious structure and identity on the other side of the divide.

  2. Others don’t see us as we see ourselves. Closely related to point number 1 is that we might want to consider how other see us. The image included with this post illustrates this well. We may see ourselves as noble messengers of God sharing a life- and soul-saving message, but many times others see as as hateful bigots. We might step back in try some perspective taking as to how our efforts are perceived by those we want to persuade.

  3. We are needlessly confrontational. There are all kinds of examples in the Bible and church history that Christians can look to in order to inform the way they share their message. I’m not sure why this aggressive and confrontational way of relating to others, especially on their sacred space, is so popular with some evangelicals. Unless of course there’s an assumption that this is the best and only way to be “biblical,” and along the way they miss the point that the Bible also includes culturally-sensitive forms of engagement as well. We might ask ourselves whether this is really appropriate and effective. As I said in a past blog post on the pageant event: “Are we being needlessly confrontational, and acting in ways which make us feel good as defenders of orthodoxy, and in the process not only losing the argument but also losing the individual?”

There’s much more that could be said, and I’d be happy to interact with anyone who wants to discuss this important topic. I hope that it at least gives some pause before the next headline making clash of religions.

items.title: OUTRAGED! by Kurt Gray, FRD senior fellow
items.body:
Kurt Gray, one of FRD’s senior fellows, has a new book out: OUTRAGED! Why We Fight About Morality and Politics and How to Find Common Ground. I have followed Gray’s work for a while, and had a podcast conversation with him before this book was written. In this volume he goes into detail and provides a multifaceted argument for harm-based morality that lies at the heart of our political and religious differences. In the past I accepted the moral foundations theory of Jonathan Haidt as seminal, but Gray’s research and argumentation made me a convert to his ideas about ingroup moral concerns related to outgroups and their competing ideologies, beliefs, and sacred values. Be sure to visit Gray’s website for the volume for additional reader information. Here’s a description of the volume:


It’s easy to assume that liberals and conservatives have radically different moral foundations. In Outraged, Kurt Gray showcases the latest science to demonstrate that we all have the same moral mind—that everyone’s moral judgments stem from feeling threatened or vulnerable to harm.

We all care about protecting ourselves and the vulnerable. Conflict arises, however, when we have different perceptions of harm. We get outraged when we disagree about who the “real” victim is, whether we’re talking about political issues, fights with our in-laws, or arguments on the playground.

In this fascinating and insightful tour of our moral minds, Gray tackles popular myths that prevent us from understanding ourselves and those around us. While it is commonly believed that our ancestors were apex predators, Gray argues that for the majority of our evolutionary history, humans were more hunted than hunter. This explains why our minds are hard-wired to perceive threats, and provides surprising insights on the scientific origins of our values and beliefs. Though we might think ourselves driven by objective reasoning, Gray unveils new research that finds our moral judgments are based on gut feelings rather than rational thought, and presents a compelling reminder that we are more alike than we might think.

Drawing on groundbreaking research, Gray provides a captivating new explanation for our moral outrage, and unpacks how to best bridge divides. If you want to understand the morals of the “other side,” ask yourself a simple question—what harms do they see?

items.title: Evangelical Zen, second edition
items.body:
FRD Senior Fellow and Evangelical chapter collaborator, Paul Louis Metzger, has worked to produce the second edition of the book Evangelical Zen, where he reflects on his journey with the late Kyogen Carlson, who headed up FRD’s Buddhist chapter. The description at the publisher’s website reads:

”Evangelical Zen is part Augustine's Confessions and part Robert Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance. Here Paul Louis Metzger, an Evangelical Christian theologian, reflects on his spiritual journey--an inner pilgrimage of sorts that weaves through a physical forty-day journey with his family to Japan. The experiences of that journey, the beauties of Japan, its culture, and its religion become for him a lens on a deeper quest: here he is searching for and, he believes, finding a global humanity in conversation with the late Zen Buddhist priest Kyogen Carlson, his Buddhist friend. This second edition includes a new foreword by esteemed missionary statesman and scholar, Thomas John Hastings, a new introduction and new concluding essay by the author, and an afterword by the acclaimed Buddhist author, Sallie Jiko Tisdale.”

Paul announced the second edition on his Facebook page with these words:

“I treasure the memories of sacred moments with my family in Japan and memorable exchanges with Abbot Kyogen Carlson that fill this book. My heart is full of gratitude for these relationships….Many thanks to all those who helped to make this second edition possible, and for the prayers and good thoughts that sustain my family on our ongoing journey. Mysteriously, Kyogen's friendship also accompanies me in my heart and thoughts.”

items.title: PBS Frontline and “A Year of War”
items.body: I recently watched an edition of PBS Frontline titled “A Year of War: Israelis and Palestinians.” I went into the program expecting political analysis, but instead watched the gut-wrenching and graphic stories of Israelis who lost loved ones when Hamas attacked on October 7, 2023, and Palestinians who lost loved ones in the Israeli response in the bombing and devastation of Gaza. The stories were so tragic, and the images of brutality so graphic, that at one point I almost turned off the program. But it is necessary to look at such violence rather than turn away if we are to deal with it. I found this use of stories compelling, much more so than any historical and political analysis. Although the responses to the mutual animosity, violence and trauma varied slightly among those who experienced it, most seemed to be in a place where the “other” was now viewed as monstrous and no forgiveness or peace possible. I came away with an even stronger emotional connection to the importance of this intractable conflict, and a desire to try to have an impact in some way through FRD’s efforts. This episode can be streamed here.

items.title: Who Blogs Here?
items.body: For the most part the leadership team at FRD will blog here.  \John Morehead and Randall Paul will be frequent contributors. FRD includes a group of Senior Advisors (see elsewhere on the FRD website) that might post from time to time. When FRD chapter directors desire to speak to a broader audience than folks in their own tradition, they will post here too. Indeed, we welcome anyone to contact John or Randall (see contact elsewhere on the FRD website) if they want to contribute here, perhaps in an open conversation with us. We won’t guarantee to publish you, but we welcome your initiatives.

items.title: Welcome to Our First Blog!
items.body: With the launch of our new and updated website we are incorporating a blog. This forum provides us with an opportunity to provide ongoing and new material. Along the way we will provide our commentary on religion items in the news, as well as share our various projects with you. We hope you find this section of the website helpful and thought provoking.

items.title: What About Extremists?
items.body: As we debate the best ways in which to address deep polarization people often have their limits for how far we should go, and which groups and individuals are beyond hope. One example is Nazis. A few years ago, various “punch a Nazi” memes circulated that suggested that this was an appropriate way of dealing with Nazis and other White Supremacists. But experts, including former White Supremacists and neuroscientists studying conflict disagree. The former is represented by Brad Galloway, who has been a guest on the Multifaith Matters podcast for the Evangelical FRD chapter. In an article he wrote that, ""I ask them how they want to better themselves, what would they want to change in their lives. To change behavior and how we look at others, it's all about re-framing the humanization of others. And eventually the ideologies break down." The late neuroscientist Emile Bruneau’s perspective compliments this insight. His research demonstrated that it was often being the recipient of undeserved kindness that fostered change, not shaming and violence.

items.title: The Power of a Shared Meal
items.body:
There’s something incredible that happens when people sit down together and break bread. Not just for friends and family, but even for people who have deep divisions and don’t like each other. There’s a growing body of literature on this topic which goes by names like “culinary diplomacy.” We have noted the power and potential, and for this reason we include a shared meal as part of our Heart & Mind Conversations. This process was incorporated a few years into in an intriguing television program called "Breaking Borders" from the Travel Channel. This unique show combined great cooking with meal conversations between enemies. Unfortunately, it was limited to one season. Click this link to watch the episode that is still timely titled Israel/Palestine at the Vimeo page of the show’s producer Brian Leonard.

WHAT IF a new series of short videos, or a series was produced, that tapped into the science of conflict and brought people together over a common meal and strategic conversations geared toward creating openness and trust-building?
items.excerpt: There’s something incredible that happens when people sit down together and break bread.

items.title: Friendship and Trusted Rivals
items.body: One of the big ideas of religious diplomacy is that we must move beyond suspicion and contempt regarding those we strongly disagree with in the area of values, worldviews, politics, and religion. Through a strategic process of interaction we believe it is not only possible to move beyond these things, but also to develop friendships that can be maintained despite differences. Years ago, we produced the video US and THEM: Religious Rivalry in America, and this hope for friendship through religious difference was expressed by the film’s narrator, Bryan Hall a Latter-day Saint, in conversation with Pastor Robert Jeffress, a Baptist Christian. As you can see in the video clip below, while Bryan was hopeful, Pastor Jeffress seems less than enthusiastic about the possibility. Even so, we hope others will join us in seeking trust-building relationships and friendships despite our differences.
